paragraphs.text: Highest and holy God, source of all power, almighty: human minds may not grasp you with their senses, however subtly they search into things, and yet it is wrong not to know you. By deep reasoning we believe that you are God in three, yet that the three are one in such a way that an undivided substance gives each its proper form, keeping the covenant in a holy bond. You alone are without beginning and likewise everlasting without end, always the same and subject to no age. However far the recesses of the mind may stretch, you go beyond the space of things, and no space encloses you. There is no place, among the things you nurture, that could contain you, and you are no more a place yourself. Nor may the mind arrive at what your likeness is, since a form bounded by no limit escapes the senses; nor at what motion quickens you with blessed power, since you are always wholly everywhere. You are mind and the innermost substance of holy mind; you are reason and the wise source of perfect reason; you are power, the summit of power, and indeed you yourself are life and the begetter of life and of deep light; you are the true light, O God, the cause and the vigor of all things. From you whatever suddenly sprang forth out of nothing took its beginning, and, filled by so great an author, it either has the power of mind or has received its form in mind. Nature, preserved even though its parts perish, proves you Lord, and the order it was given confesses the sequence you commanded. You distinguish obedient numbers, balance weights, vary measures and govern rhythm and motion. You command things to keep their alternating turns and their unceasing round to stand firm, and you bid the ages, set moving by you in the ether, now roll on a world full of the image of mind. You were not content to endow with a single gift whatever created thing comes through you into use. Rather, a thing that is made is something more, all things are better in the part where they lie hidden, and an inner cause also makes things pleasing in themselves please. Some things have sharpened their vigor from others; certain opposites have more peace if they contend. So, rich Creator, you bind all things together as kin, even through opposing elements, and fill them with powers poured out from the whole. And yet, though these things lie within your majesty of creating, you need none of the things you beget. The work of the world, completed and abiding through you in a stable framework of things, does not run on for your sake but stands ready as a gift to us. All things are within your power. Nor does your glory lie only in this, that as a good author you make things that bestow benefits, but in this too, that you make them able to bestow benefits themselves: you enfold secondary causes in the first, so that whoever experiences your gifts is himself also your gift. You have shown by clear reasoning that goodness alone, O God, was your reason for commanding all things to come into being. When you first bade spirits to live and to enjoy the world that you bore in your mind, being was given to things suddenly made; they spread far and wide into heaven and earth together, and you offered a shining dwelling to the angelic flock. To them you granted, with a kindly mind, free hearts and the power to choose for themselves, so that virtue might become a work of their own, and so that you might confer this also on the merits of the godly, becoming a debtor by your very giving. One of those you first created to reign envied the Lord of light and life, his own author, and coveted that title; he chose to be the author of evil and to bring death upon the earth, and was cast down from lofty heaven with his partners in crime. Yet it is not right on that account to lay any charge against the holy power, for which it is enough to have made what is good. Nor was it right that anyone should lack God's gift (and in this lies the sum of his kindly praise), or that even the ungrateful should be denied life and sense and the mind's own sovereignty in all its affairs. For what profit is there in created beings unless they have a free mind? And no one has a truly free mind unless he is allowed to perish. That this freedom had been granted no one would have proved except by sinning. To this I would add that all things, set against their opposites, hold one another in a mutual test; and that the possibility of perishing was therefore given to all, so that living might be sweeter, and the equal measure of a shared and alternating peril might count toward merit, when the punishment of the wicked, worthy of a stern judge, would double the rewards of the saints. Or else — Father, may I be allowed to say this, trembling, having first asked your leave — perhaps in your sight there is more good in the good not having sinned through the slippery times of life than there is evil in the wretched having sinned. But let your majesty see to how the judgment to come shall stand. This is enough for us: that through you, breathing the noble work of reason into earth, you raised up man from vile dust, so that even such a creature might conquer the enemy who was ungrateful to his Lord. And when man had been dragged by the deceit of a cruel poison into the snares of death and down to impious Tartarus, you soon deigned to take a body and sought him out with your own blood from the abodes of Erebus; you restore him with greater care than when he was made, give him back to everlasting life, and carry him with you into heaven, the enemy subdued. Now, then, let no one rashly blame father Adam because, in breaking a light precept and violating the law, he opened the road to death. That first punishment of our parent was worth so much, because it is a greater thing to conquer death than never to have known death. Now, rejoicing, he looks down from the hall of his homeland on the vaults of heaven, treads upon the stars, and calls to the kingdom to come the ministers appointed for it, whom the Wisdom of the Father's Word, which begot the universe, formed anew by water and taught to be born again. In him I pray to you, kindly God, who by your gracious power give understanding to souls and compel hearts to speak the truth even when the prophet does not know it: grant me, as I pray, to know what the renowned scrolls of Moses the lawgiver unfold, while I set about shaping tender minds and hearts in their boyhood years for the true path of virtue: what the origin of the heavens is, or what the first beginnings of the world; how a growing plague shook hidden faith out of the whole world and error sank deep into morals; and by what way truth returns again, drives out profane rites, and unlocks the mystic sacraments of eternal life. Give me also the mind, give the mind fitting times, give zeal, so that care may not fail so great a labor; and give good sense to my study, and that which rightly runs over all known things and encloses them in a strong covering [?]. And do not condemn me merely because I, so guilty, dare so great a task. Kindly forgive all the sins I have committed; you have given souls strength and sense and merit too. But if the arrangement of my words should offend at all against the law of meter, if improper diction and wavering sense should go astray (let it be permitted to run on here and there in careless verse), let no danger to the faith creep in from this measure, through Christ [?], who, your only Son, flourishing with you in majesty equally with the kindly Spirit, lives and reigns for ages of ages beyond the grasp of minds, which the solemn Amen consecrates to you.
BOOK ONE.
Before the poles, before the daylight of the sky and the darkness of the world,
before the shapes of his works, before things or the seeds of things,
(eternal without end looking back, without end looking forward,
he to whom being always belongs) there was one God, with whom
lived the begotten Word, God, and with them the nurturing
Spirit, the life-giving sum of hidden power.
By this bond the one substance of the Three, quickening itself,
blessed itself forever with unbegotten power
and reigned in might. In the majesty of creating
he already saw things, and the causes of things, and events to come,
and all that was to be made and begotten; with capacious mind
he surveyed the ages, and whatever the times unroll
he held ever present. Immense in his blessed greatness,
he was his own kingdom, nor did his kingdom lack a witness,
God, the threefold power, who first, from no seed,
giving bodies to things as he compelled things to exist,
so as to make a gift for us—a work that he alone possessed,
he alone knew—brought forth at once all that completes
the wealthy world; but, producing them in parts and marking them off
by a fixed boundary, he brought them out each in its proper origin,
so that order, set in motion in a sequence, might now found time.
For it was not—as the tongue of sacrilegious madness held—
mindless chance, rolling unknowing seeds about,
that twisted together so wise a work; nor is it right to say that the world was born
before day, since things born in time are subject to motion,
and then there was no time; nor to believe that, eternal
into the past, it has always held a stable vigor;
for what consists of bodies must be admitted to have had a beginning.
For a body, which a blow wears down, which time dissolves
and abolishes by the very end toward which it tends,
shows that it had a beginning, since things shown to have received their lot
are rightly believed to have been made, or thought to have been born.
For the things that are born are carried along, moving with time;
[?] times, running on after the mass of the world, are born
from what is prior. And they must consist of bodies; [?]
they prove it could not have been [?]; they confess it could have been made.
It is agreed, therefore, that the world was made: everyone, compelled,
assents to this and, convinced by true doctrine, believes it;
he concedes that God made it, who by the power of the Word
and mighty in strength arranged whatever is reckoned as nature,
commanded it, admonished it; and the gift he created,
ever renewing fleeting things in successive turns,
he sustains, and, drawing it back, wheels the swift orb around.
And should he wish to dissolve the whole in an instant,
he could take being away from things—and not only this present being:
by a reason he alone knows, he could take from the past the very fact that they had been.
O how great the might of the Father, how great the glory of the Word!
What measure is there in the whole, what sum in the gift, when
the vault of the lofty sky and the outspread lands
are only the first part of the work? But the sea had covered the lands,
and the air in between, dripping with filthy cloud,
the blind shadow of the sky pressed down with dense darkness.
And the holy Spirit, hovering over the outstretched waves,
enlivened the nourishing waters, and the seeds of things,
to be poured out into shoots once the lands were set in order,
he gave to be instilled in them—when light, sent from above,
flashed forth at God's command, and the shadow, divided off, drawing back
its black robe, departed from highest heaven,
and set the waters [?] in between, and, fleeing the light that pursued it,
was soon behind its back. Thus the limit of day gave a name
to the spans of light, and, poured back upon the world,
the interrupted darkness made a night equal to it.
Again a new morning: the first evening now driven off,
light returned and shone, when a most firm mass,
stretching itself out from the midst of the waves with solidified body,
rose up and, made solid far and wide with hard rigidity,
held the divided waters suspended, and set the cold deep
against the hot poles of heaven, and, resting on the sea it had enclosed,
spread itself over the things that it shut in
with its vast circuit, and stripped the ancient sky of its name.
Perhaps someone here may reason thus with himself, in learned error:
so that the heavenly fires may not lack fuel,
and excessive heat, seeking the depths in pursuit of nourishment,
may not burn up the mortal race, and earthly things may not be unable
to endure the flashing sky, the firm frame of heaven
has been set below, which, while it shields us with shade, [?]
is itself veiled with waters. But, my mind, flee far
from seeking such causes: let it be enough for you always to believe
that God can do whatever is thought impossible.
And that the great sea is borne above the stars and constellations,
prove by the reasoning of those very people who refuse to believe it
and yet would have the world hang suspended—the world which its Founder himself,
governing it always by a reason beyond comprehension,
carries and turns, holding it steady despite its immense weight.
The third light was astonished to see the swelling billows withdraw,
when God, driving back the waves of the remaining flood,
opened a great void in the spaces of the air.
Then for the first time the dry, lowest part of the world showed
its uncovered face, and, trembling at the power of the Word,
the blue seas girded the lands laid bare.
These, bidden to grow green at once with varied offspring,
luxuriant shoots covered from the fresh soil,
and the young forest, bursting from the tender turf,
tossed its joyful foliage and its very fruits,
and each, bearing its own seed, bore witness to its Sower.
Now, three days completed, kindled by swift motion
and bidden to gather itself into flames and a globe of fire,
came the first day of the sun, and the seeds of light, now established,
scattered crimson tresses from a rosy blaze;
and the moon, the glory of the night—whether it shone with its own light
or, struck by the approaching globe, poured back its rays—
hung on a lower path, set beneath the sun;
and that the stars, painting the world in distinct zones,
quivered with varied colors like flowers of the sky,
and that heaven shone the more for its adorned darkness,
the blue night was astonished, while their shafts, poured out with ruddy flames,
flicker, and the new constellations eagerly press on their casts.
These the sun's splendor overcasts with its rays, and with a kind of night
made of deep light it hides them; and, dividing the seasons
marked off by a fixed boundary, completing its fixed station,
bidden to return in the measured turns of the headlong sky,
bidden once to set out, it completes the revolving year
and by its wondrous structure confesses its holy Craftsman.
The fifth day set breathing bodies moving in the sea,
which the water readily begot and scattered through the deep,
the delights of the ocean, which in varied kinds and wondrous
ways nature formed—nature which, bidden to create,
compels even the parts of things to live for themselves in place of the whole,
and gave the soul leave to pass into brute shapes;
and creatures whose scaly backs, in the flood of the swelling brine,
would grow without end, stuffed with soft fat,
did not a swift limit prescribe a bound to their vast span of life.
The life-giving water itself favors the bodies of its nurslings,
the water which also nourishes the seed of the earth, but rather dissolves
the heaped-up limbs that moisture had stretched too far.
From this the birds too, a delicate race, drew their vigor.
While he shapes the flowing waters, and life, sent into the sea,
enters it, the swelling seas seethe again with a brood
not born for themselves; and presently, sent forth from the deep,
a scaly throng, as it rises to the surface of the waves,
having flown through the water, little by little swims through the clear air
and shows that it can reach the recesses of the sky—
this creature, which is born a second time from the shining waves.
Now the sixth day was shining in bright heaven,
the third after the life-giving gifts of the warm sun,
and now the warming earth had loosened its pregnant limbs,
when God, intent on greater things, bade the earth bring forth
every animal that only the power of motion quickens,
whose lot is to serve wherever the needs of things require.
No delay: from the fruitful lands burst forth living
offspring, each allotted the shapes of its own kind,
now in need of a master, for whose sake he had prepared all things,
he who alone is able to create even what is yet to be made.
From here let me be permitted to touch some things lightly,
to pass over some altogether in an anxious, hurried course,
and to relate some I have passed over in altered order.
After the appointed order had brought forth all things according to their kinds,
things which, at God's command, full then of the Father's mind,
the almighty Son made, and which the Holy Spirit approved
as full of true goods and laden with rich endowment,
and cherished, that they might endure in long succession,
a nearer cause is given to the world, for which the world in turn
was the rightful prior cause. Already the world existed, already the stars and their risings,
the upper air, the glassy sea and the green lands:
but if no beholder is present whom the glory of so great a fabric
may fill, leading his eager eyes through each and every thing,
what could they offer to God? There is no possession
if the possessor of things is absent. Then the Ruler of heaven:
"The work has reached its sum; good are all the things that I have created.
Now let us make man," he says, "to reign over the world
and to be the image of God. It is fitting that he be like his Creator,
since, free in his choice, he will enjoy created things with a mind."
He had spoken, and man was made—whether as a whole body
without soul and form, perhaps in the way in which he makes future things
and things yet to be made, the way in which he always held as already made
what had not yet come about in an age almost past [?].
And soon he set him over all things and bade him, with his wife,
increase through offspring and fill the empty lands.
And now, as God thus spoke his blessing, the power of procreation
was laid upon all things that move with life of their own.
The seventh light saw that the great Father had ceased,
but had ceased only from creating the number of kinds,
and had kept his rest; and rightly it was hallowed,
since it saw a different work; for this too is full
of power: that God ceased and laid down his labors.
As a pattern for his offspring, by which they might earn worthy rewards,
it is enough that the Lord looked upon twice three days of work:
the seventh light taught a venerable example of rest,
which he bids the peoples hope for as the reward of their life,
to be granted forever once the works of the godly are done.
This too is that light on which Christ broke open dread Tartarus
and, having conquered Avernus, opened the way of return,
while he rested in the earth, about to return to his Father's hall.
So God knows how to cease, so he knows how to take his leisure,
that in ceasing he does more. Resting without end
and equally working without end, blending succession and time,
by ceasing he completes the work, whatever he had created,
so as to make it, and first to endow man now with a body,
man who was last—for to found the causes of things
is not the same as giving limbs—or else, since the seventh day so runs on
that the sixth day also remains, because the sixth is surely
the same as the first to God, who has all things ever present
that slip away from us, after any lapse of time whatever the supreme
Author still thus fashions man on the sixth day;
or else, to teach that we rightly surpass created things,
we whom he makes with his own hand, he declares more plainly
now that man was made, and makes this known to the solid world:
"All things that move with a soul were brought forth at a command;
you, by the working of God." Who could offer to so great a Father
rites of praise worthy of him, who unfolded the world and all things
in an instant by his command, and while he commanded, brought their being to pass?
Us he brings into being with deliberation; around us he deigns to spend
the care of holy effort, and resolves to carry out
what is almost a work of toil; for the clay, which readily yields
and bends and follows the shape into which art draws it,
he takes up and unfolds into the very form he already bore
in his holy mind; and, breathed in with warm breath,
life watered the soil. The earth, softened with moisture,
became in part flesh: blood, a slippery fluid,
swells the soft veins through their familiar channels;
and now man is full of mind, and, thrust off from the earth,
he leaps up and, endowed with reason, adores his Lord.
Not otherwise, true faith holds, will bodies rise at command from their burst tombs,
when the Majesty, gliding down from the opened heaven,
unlocks the hollow womb of the pregnant earth.
For since the earth, lacking any power of its own, brought forth
what it did not have, when thus from the surface dust
God gave it shape, it is easy for it, at the word of the same Judge,
to give back what it received at his command. So the whole of what was first begotten
is a figure of what is to come; and while Adam himself is formed in such a way
that the narrative, told twice over, doubles the holy gift,
it is usefully foreshown that peoples will one day be born again.
Their source and supreme origin being then given,
where the blessed land opens up its eastern recesses,
on a loftier rise a paradise of pleasant grove
is planted and laid out with rows of shapely trees.
Here, where the sun's boundary is now divided in equal spaces
and an eternal spring tempers the year with equal hours,
there each tree stands rich with its own fruits,
and ripe fruits are pushed off by the fruits that follow,
which, pleasing to the eye and full of wondrous vigor,
refresh body and spirit and nourish them with taste and scent.
The earth, many-hued, flickers with starry colors
in ever-new flowers; and plants which, dry in withered sheaths,
now shed their brittle stalks, quickened by the vigor
of an ambrosial gift, pour forth fragrant cinnamon;
nor do the scent the Mede breathes out, or the fragrance
of the Achaemenian with his loosened hair, or of the Assyrian rich in soft amomum,
or of the Mareotic harvest red with nard,
of the shrubs of Tartessus, of the Sabaean twig,
and what the Palestinian branch weeps from its torn wound,
fail to pour into the air, each with its different savor.
For God gathered here together, all alike, and brought back
the things that nature had received one by one in fixed places;
and while the grove, stirred, quivers in the gentle current of the breeze,
it blends one nectar out of the diverse scents,
and a new gift arises, which no tree can claim as its own;
and wherever, trembling, gently tossed with a soft rustling,
it quivers with stirring leaves, the forest sounds in every tree
a hymn to God, and the breeze whistles its measured
songs: nor does any empty motion shake the air in vain,
since with the Author, who holds the whole within one fabric,
binding thing to thing, and keeps it by a law of exchange,
nothing is idle, nor does any form hold an empty shape.
And perhaps the grove itself and the gleaming woods
are the patterns of works and the nurseries of things,
and what comes into human life as a bare name
has there a definite body and blossoms on its own stem:
glory, simplicity, zeal, vigilance, sleep,
care, safety, terror, eloquence, grace, motion
and feeling, the spurs of the soul, watchfulness, virtue,
and all that the world has—because it is born there,
it thrives here, and stirs minds and supplies the senses.
But it is enough for faith that, rising from joyful seed,
on one side the tree of life reaches into the air with lofty fruits,
and on the other, knowledge, harmful with its different fruit,
has hung the testing of things on the tree of the law.
But the heart of the holy grove, which the forest crowns,
a spring waters, and with rich power weds it to offspring,
joyfully releasing its swelling source in a fourfold river,
richer than Ocean; for this spring, ready with unceasing flood,
gives waters of its own, while Ocean receives all waters
and does not feel them. Lesser is he who cannot grow
though such floods pour into him than he who cannot diminish
though rivers pour out of him. But in the first stream the Pishon
leaps forth exulting, a fourth part of the blessed spring,
displaying in its nature the endowments that prudence gives;
it fills the peoples of the Ganges, and the realms of Havilah
it swells with silt, and, rolling along lands and seeds,
sows the fields it makes. Where it lies rough with bare sands,
amid golden flakes of glittering metal
the carbuncle flashes, glowing with lightning fire,
and the emerald gleams, radiant with green light.
Nor is the Gihon lesser, coming from there, but, gentler with its placid waves,
it raises the waters of the Nile and covers far and wide
with a kindly flood the fields that would burn, and, resisting the sky,
tempers the air of the Ethiopians with its pools as they flow back.
Third from here, running forth with rapid flood, the Tigris
goes as companion to the Euphrates; as they rush on in a single mass,
the earth, overcome, gapes open and swallows them in a hollow abyss,
until, into the glades of Armenia and the pastures of Media,
it vomits forth the rivers it could not bear and can hold no longer.
But the Tigris, as if indignant at black Avernus,
leaps forth with greater force into the air of heaven,
and again goes under into caves, and, plunged into caverns,
roars within, and, made stronger by the barrier,
swells with waters, and, swifter from the narrow cave,
it issues forth and cleaves the Assyrian plains with its rapid column.
More just is the Euphrates, which, generous with rich flood,
waters the parched fields of Persia lying below it,
drawn off in gentle channels, and serves all alike
and offers itself wholly to human use,
until, drained of its waters, in its prodigality it spends even its very name
upon the lands, which it owed to the waves of the sea.
These realms, then, rich with every offspring of nature,
these delights, filled with so many and such great endowments of power,
are the first possession of the first man,
into which he had been led and bidden to rejoice in perpetual life
as its dweller: and now, amid these first gifts,
while he is still becoming worthy and learning by effort to deserve
what he possesses, having gained the fruit of full virtue,
he lived free of cares and knowing nothing of longing.
So much merit does it count with the Author, in place of the highest title,
to have not yet deserved anything evil. How much, then, do we think
the Father can pay out for the life that will return in time,
when even then his first largesse to his servants
was paradise, not wages? And in bringing those decrees of a strict
law and curbing freedom,
he still promises greater things to the good and keeps rewards in store,
he who established a ground for merit when he said: "Eat
of all the trees; this one alone remember to dread,
which, bearing the testing of opposite things,
will make you know that you knew the good only when, wounded by a profane bite,
it makes you know evil—and the penalty of death will follow."
By giving such a law, the Father's deep design teaches
that he willed man not to become mortal, but to live, and to be worthy,
worthy—a worthiness that a little obedience
would bring about. O how great is the kindness of the great God!
What he bestows on his servants of his own kindly will, he wishes
to become a work deserving our praise, the fruit of our own labor,
and he would rather that what he gives should seem to be owed.
But you, whom the guardianship of holy law binds,
do not complain that your liberty, shut within narrow limits,
is robbed of part of itself: nothing has been cut away from you by this law.
Before, you had obtained power only over land and sea;
now you hold power over the kingdom and over everlasting life,
and now over death as well. Then, so that the untaught dweller in the world
might believe that the loving Father had granted all things to him,
every animal that the earth, bidden to bring forth, had created
and poured out from silent seed, quickening into bodies,
God commanded to come and obey its own sovereign,
and Adam to pronounce the highest titles of the kinds, so as to fix
names on their species as on things that serve him:
Adam, who at the Lord's prompting, amid such great gifts of life,
gave to each its proper name as well. No delay: nature presents
to God every kind, from whatever part of the new world
it was created. Creatures so different in motion gather together
in the space of a single moment: those strong in effort,
slow with soft step, most nimble with rapid running,
those whom the Father fitted either to glide headlong through the air
in a plunging rush or, buoyed on the seas, to slip along under their own weight,
he equipped, bestowing diverse gifts,
and armed them with hand, horn, hoof, tooth, venom,
and other means with which he fortified the solid frame
of creatures lacking skill and of lesser mind. But none of the living creatures
flourished with an aspect equal to man's, in face and bearing,
and, set beside him, they only added to his honor;
and among so many that brighten life with their twofold sex
he alone was unpaired, he who had long held within himself,
unknowing, the fitting material for bringing forth a wife.
So God undertakes the well-known work, and, suddenly striking
the man's heart, loosens it, drowsy, in so deep a sleep
that from him, bereft of consciousness, he might in his power draw out a rib,
while the flesh, commanded, rises to follow, and the skin, drawing back
along with the bone, leaves no gap between [?]—
taking it with limbs unharmed and body sound.
The rib, spreading out, soon distributed through various limbs,
received a form and, animated with warm marrow,
took on the work of life, now pleasing in the second sex,
and, given to her husband, was named Eve.
Here now, most foolish crowd, cease at last
to presume to set your judgment in anything above the holy Father,
asking why the first woman was formed thus from the limbs
of her husband, when she could have been fashioned from soft dust,
or even from nothing. This surely is the true reason:
lest a natural order should rather claim [?] for itself,
or because man is from man, and it should lie open to the clear world [?]
that all things were then made together, so that a certain kinship
might blend mutual love with care for oneself,
compelling each to recognize himself in the other's limbs.
Hence it is that Adam, unknowing, felt that he had
received back a part of himself: a new grace touched his mind,
and affection, received through his eyes, rushed into the familiar
inward parts and pierced his very bones with such heat
that it now gave him to know that "wife" is the name of a spouse,
that children are sweet, and that parents must be placed after
spouses. What then? Now the two would have remained in one flesh,
leading an eternal life together—
for so long as they were free of the vices and stain of the earth,
they flourished with godlike souls, needing none
of the riches the world offered: for they did not bear bodies
subject to disease, nor were they nurslings of a greedy belly;
food was only for delight, and what need demands
was not yet a prop of life, and the soul's own immortality
was in full vigor—had not the dread serpent, goaded by the venom
of a greater evil, persuaded unwary Eve to break the law
with deceits such as these:
"O mortals, deprived of a better life, a race ignorant
of good things! For he who does not know how to discern
how opposite things differ from the good does not know the good either.
And that is why God did not wish it lawful for man to pluck
these august fruits, lest, once the cloud was lifted from the mind,
they should give eyes to souls, and, as to what is best, the other
part of things, teaching all secrets, should make men skilled
and like gods." Here now let me be permitted to digress a little
and lament the shameful ruin of the ancients.
Ah, pagans, too wretched, whom madness drove
into various rites! It is plain in what death the profane
utterly perished. The plural name of "gods"
was first sounded by the impious voice of the dread serpent,
who was then the cause of death. For after credulous Eve
had broken the command with sacrilegious bites,
now schooled by the experience of evil, she looks for comfort in her guilt,
and, meaning to draw her compliant husband into the crime,
assails him with the very art by which she had first perished. So, overcome by a twofold
enemy, wretched Adam yields to the crime
and tasted the fruit, most alluring with its sacred juice.
But because beneath it lay the commands of a strict law,
bringing death more surely than a viper's venom,
as soon as they had defiled their bodies with the forbidden taste,
at once they felt their wrongdoing, and the deed they had done
grew and struck their hearts with a feeling unknown before.
Hence fear, hence shame: for before, it had been granted them to live naked
and not know it—whether because, full of nourishing vigor,
these simple humans, aware of lofty things, bearing hearts
intent only on heaven and the universe,
their breasts ever turned toward the exalted Father,
while they observed the wonders of divine secrets
by the splendor of an almost bodiless mind,
had not yet come to care for their own limbs,
heedless of them by reason of a better soul; or because no impulse
could penetrate bodies that no lapse of time would dissolve into old age,
an impulse that would make them aware of whatever is necessary.
After that everlasting vigor of life had deserted
what was now a mortal creature, then at last cold and heat,
the changes of the air, came upon them, and see—the humans felt
that they needed clothing, and in secret blushed
for their sex. Lamenting wretchedly with silent
tears, they weave new coverings from leaves of the shady fig,
stitched together—coverings which, veiling the body, would only lay bare
the shame their minds had taken on after their guilt.
Nor was this enough for the frightened pair. What were they to do, how escape
the crime branded on them, and themselves? They would have wished, if it could open,
to bury themselves in the earth: so close is guilt
to its own punishment that now, dreading mortality,
the wretched find comfort in the image of death. Forests and shady thickets
they put between themselves and God, the false comforts of an empty hiding place.
For where may you withdraw your timid body,
you—you, I say, Adam, who will soon be the first to be dragged back?
The living, most hidden power of the Father, everywhere present, fills the world
and, spreading out, passes beyond its boundless recesses.
But truly it is wrong to cheat the frightened of a refuge:
that man can escape the supreme Lord by fleeing
who flees to the Lord; if you abandon him even in mind alone,
[you will see] in what vast darkness you lie, and yet are not hidden [?].
calling aloud, “Where are you?”, he bears witness to both at once.
For why does God, who sees you, look for you? And why, when you will always
be present to him, when not even death itself, which you underwent
through the frailty of your mind, can steal you away from him,
why does he ask where you are, unless it is because, in the manner of grief,
he declares that you, having fallen of your own will, are no longer with him
and have fallen from holy heaven? But the holy love of the Father
forbids despair, for his mercy —
let me be allowed to say it, and allowed too to prove what I have said —
surpasses his justice. Nor, when he rebukes me with a stern voice,
asking where I am and what I am turning over in my trembling heart,
does he so much hold [?] me as revive me, for even after my crimes he calls me,
fallen, sunk in fear, in hiding and almost buried,
he calls me out and calls me back. No need to search for examples far afield:
the very pardon of the guilt proves the Lord is gentle.
After the searching inquiry had singled out the chief culprits,
the Almighty begins — heaven, sea and earth tremble as he speaks,
and, shaken, lay open their vast recesses,
and the sentence that punished the guilty created Tartarus —:
“Since you thought it safe to depart from our commands,
in the same order in which the guilt ran its course of crime
my just censure shall strike the new offenders.
Among all the creatures I bade enjoy the whole world
you shall be accursed, and worse than the envious mind you hide within,
you serpent, who cast down human beings created to enter heaven
and, driving them by your deceit to touch the forbidden fruit,
became the origin of bitter death.
So that a fitting measure of punishment may follow the wickedness:
you plunged human beings into the earth; you too, your limbs stretched on the hostile ground,
shall furrow the hard earth with your breast;
you made them sin through food; for such daring
you too shall forever eat the filthy bowels of the earth.
And since it pleased you, as befits you, to be the first
inventor of death, you shall die a bloody death;
and arming the hatred of the human race especially
against your whole kind, you that are steeped in savage venom,
I will ordain that you be always feared, so that you may be destroyed the more.
And as for this woman, whom you rejoice to have overcome by your first deceit,
you shall live beneath her feet, crawling on your breast,
and lie in wait only for the soles of her feet,
while she, though trembling, shall plant her footsteps on your head.”
He spoke, and then began thus against Eve, pale as death:
“But you, who thought that to destroy the fruit by yourself alone
was the least part of the crime, and then with a mind bent on harm
laid a trap for your wretched husband and gained mastery through so great a crime,
shall bow to a servile yoke, and in subjection you shall feel
the will of a harsh husband, and suffer toils
with constant mishaps, so that you, who first dared
to multiply the wickedness once begun, may be tossed among many perils;
and in childbirth you shall be so tormented by frequent offspring
that those whom your guilt will cause to be born mortal
shall sometimes be the cause of a mangled death for their mother.”
“You too, who dared to set our warnings and the first
bonds of salvation below a woman’s deceits,
and chose to die of your own will, receive, guilty one, this lot:
let the earth, which you shall furrow with the plough,
be cursed for your crimes. Let it bear thorns and menacing thistles
even when tilled, and let a cruel hope cheat your prayers. You ceased to serve me with a faithful mind:
let not the earth keep faith with you. You refused of your own will
to live happily amid these delights and to live through all the ages:
now live in hard labour,
live in misery, until slow old age
makes you earth — which is more truly what you are — and pours you back into the earth.”
He spoke, and in pity covered with the skins of beasts those who did not know
how to shield their limbs from the weather, and taught them
to protect their lives. But lest Adam, stirred by fear of death,
should dare again the crime he was harbouring in his mind;
lest, ignorant of how things stood, he should seek once more from the tree of life,
after his cause had reached its last extremity, the proud help
that was his by original right, and so live on, redeemed by no art of the Father,
and the mystic order should then totter for the world,
and heavier woes should await the wretched, forever guilty pair —
at once, when they were ordered to leave the sacred groves,
winds stirred up by the depths of the forest
carried them away — yet the bearing breeze held them fast
in a balancing whirlwind, and the wind swept up the whole air
as nature bent its course — and brought them back to the earth
from which their bodies had been given, and set them down with a softened blast,
unharmed by so great a distance and unharmed by danger,
but not spared the grief that troubles the heart.
Where they have fallen, what they have lost, what life lies ahead,
what life had been — a sad comparison torments their minds
and heaps up the contrasts all the more; and they ponder within themselves
how different they now are, how changed each one
seeks his own self, unsure whether to ascribe this to the first guilt
and its punishment — that their error forced them to know the power of evil —
or whether this is what it is to die; or, if heavier woes remain,
whether the wretched will be granted a return, or whether in an everlasting end
they will lose what remains; or whether, since the way of bitter death
has burst upon the world and upon peoples to come through a tree,
life might yet somehow return through a tree.
BOOK TWO.
So far I have run through the hidden order of things, the beginnings of the world,
as sincere faith revealed it, without deceit,
while earthly things were still free of the vices that deserve death.
Now that he has come in his verse to the ways of men and to things now mortal,
let the poet be allowed to blend them with the truth.
After the two of them, ordered to leave the sacred
seats and realms, reached the fields where they had been made
and stood as exiles on their own soil — a pitiable sight! — with what
faces the untaught tillers then stare in stupor at the wild countryside,
which bears no bloom adorned with fruit-bearing trees.
No beauty of the land delights them; it is a brute heap
of packed weight, its bulk set down with no design.
The heights are stiff with rock, the hollows labor under forests,
the plains lie hidden in grass, the uplands bristle with thorns.
Alas, with what eyes do they look on these things, with what heart do they see them,
they in whose minds paradise still dwells! Nor is there only
one cause of grief, that a face full of every evil
now opens before them, but that they remember the good.
Now the glory of that sacred grove shines with a greater
brightness, now the blessed wood brings forth its riches
more abundantly, now the enjoyment of its fruits is sweeter
and their taste more like nectar; now the earth breathes with living flowers
and stings the sorrowing pair with a fragrance that is absent.
O paradise, how unlike your deserts is the return you make!
Comparison with worse things exalts you all the more,
and you make worse the things that alone remain to the wretched.
Here the kindly love of life dies away; the want of everything
now whispers that it is sweet to die, unless a greater need
came to the rescue with a heavier evil; for, inflaming their bowels
with a frenzy to eat, it drives them, ravenous, through every
fare the barren wood provides, and forces them to try
as food doubtful meals here and there from the noxious roots
of plants; and hunger itself makes them unable
to escape such a life, though it was hunger that drove them to wish it.
At last, needy of everything that use requires
and destitute of all things, they were taught by their utter extremity
to hope for the help of the supreme Father. Both, prostrate,
limbs on the ground, with only tears and mute grief,
while shame withholds words from unjust complaints,
lie as though dying of exhaustion. But when their minds returned,
Adam, rising at last, pleads with this prayer:
"Almighty author of the world and creator of all things,
woe is me for the stain of sin! While my happy life remained
and it was granted me to follow my swift thoughts with my sight beyond the stars,
you, poured out far around and through all things
forever, and veiling yourself from sight with the splendor you put forth,
I saw with these eyes — as though they were beholding the secrets of the mind —
and saw, as is fitting to say, that you cannot be seen.
Now too, after our fault, though we are stripped of sacred light,
though the better mind, once free to range through the whole,
has fled, and, shut in the cave of our earthly prison,
we have nothing of truth left to know but mortal things,
this alone has remained to us: to feel that all things are full of you.
And therefore, Almighty, you who are always wholly everywhere,
we flee to you, praying with trembling hearts:
hear the wretched, whom you always see and hear,
if, when he wished to bind me to the condemned party —
he, the head of crimes, guilty before the world and his own enemy,
who dared nothing by himself alone, lest he withdraw defeated —
the wretched woman, whose mind was unwary, through the serpent's art,
and me through the affection that both sexes feel,
were overcome by the unforeseen fraud of the craftsman of crimes;
and if, when I was condemned to a just penalty for my crime,
I so repented of my fault, and my mind, struck with such grief,
was so indignant with itself, that I thought you, most gentle judge,
were then granting me vengeance on myself.
For that reason I refused groans and tears to plead my cause,
because I, the guilty one, judged myself unworthy of pardon;
and, embracing in my heart the sweet consolations of the penalty
and henceforth counting this very thing among your sacred gifts,
I shall regard the fact that I am condemned as the pardon of my crime.
So it is not dreadful. But with serene majesty
deign to hear us, who pray for nothing against your commands
and no longer beg with tears — though in your kindness you would freely
grant it to your servants — that the censure be relaxed,
but rather that the whole sentence may keep its full force.
You ordered me to seek my food by turning the clod;
so tools for turning the condemned fields
must be given. The fields are to yield barren thickets and clinging thorns
instead of fruit; so I must first sow pure seed,
that the crop sought with toil may cheat my hopes,
and make my bread from the steady seed of plants:
grant my mind to know which plants they are, what the manner of the work;
grant help, Father, in your pity, and instruct our senses.
Then it will be that, mistress of things and sure of survival,
Eve may serve me and, having known the cruel punishment of childbearing,
may bear peoples who for our crime
will be punished; and that succession, purging the fathers' sins
by the deaths of their descendants, may make the penalty everlasting."
As they prayed thus, the image of the false serpent,
seen as fear pointed it out, gliding along a silent path
smoothly toward the soft stretches, the grasses quivering,
turned the trembling pair toward it, and, shaking them out of the stupor
of sluggish grief, drew them into a kindred wrath.
And Eve was first to speak to her husband: "If the ultimate cause of our woes
moves you, snatch up stones in your hand; look, the chance is given
to deal death to the author of death. She ought to be the first
to teach, by her own torments and a bloody death,
how grim it is to die — she who wickedly destroyed both me and you."
She spoke, and as it slips away they pursue it at a run with missile
weapons and hurl rocks; and one of them, the arm drawn back
higher for an easy throw, sure in its aim,
obeys their wishes, following their eyes and their will,
and, striking through the serpent, rebounds onto the bare flint
and strikes a spark, which, fed on dry tinder,
soon became a flame, spreading its fiery-haired blaze
far and wide, and now blossoms bright amid the dry smoke.
They had shuddered and were seeking hiding places with trembling steps,
but their very stupor holds them in their fear, and reveals the shrewd curiosity
of human weakness, in that even the fearful wish to see again
what is to be feared; and, standing a little way off
on a ridge of barren earth, they marvel that the shady
tresses of the groves have fallen, that all is grimy with ashes,
that the day is darkened, that all the lands shine
and there is a new light beneath the sun. Nor with a quiet mind
do they take in the crackling as the woods hiss on every side
and billowing balls of flame are borne up toward the stars,
while the devouring fire, sinking deep, reaches down to the lowest
roots far within; and, overcome by the heat it has absorbed,
the raw earth opens its veins to yield noble gifts,
and, when it has been dried of all its moisture,
itself begins to turn liquid and to pour out metals in streams,
each in its own. In a tawny torrent flashes
gold, highest in honor; gleaming like white milk
silver flows out; the hardness of copper wanders in slippery streams,
and steel, a livid clod, melts its body and runs together
into a soft mass. So Etna, its furnaces burst open,
pours out hissing sulphur mingled with flames,
slippery while they seethe; but when they feel the mildness
of the breathable air, they stiffen, and swiftly the dry liquid
turns into a glittering clod, its fire frozen,
and becomes an inert body. So they marvel to see the streams
halt their various courses; and these, where the heat gives out,
they now gaze on with eager eyes, and they take their alluring color
into their hands, and pursue what they had feared.
They felt God's help and rejoice that the first prayers of the guilty,
though no virtue had followed their fault,
had turned out as they wished; and to the supreme Father
they credit both what the fire gave and the fire itself
and the understanding to which he revealed its use. Two things
I hold for certain: that our first parents explored the sacred gift,
eagerly measuring everything with their eyes, but that first
they laid their hands on the rich gold, which even now strikes minds
like lightning and subdues them with the gleam of a precious poison,
and does not satisfy until it overpowers its admirers with its great weight
and, slipping from their grasp, wounds them like the sharp point of a hard rock,
and teaches them that, with bodies now corrupted, they can easily
suffer a wound. A new concern suddenly came over
the astonished pair and sharpened their minds, and chance, as teacher,
prompts them to follow it with skill. Then with the weight of hard stone
they strike by turns, and bend and draw out
the mass, which yields to the blows, into various shapes.
It takes no effort to shape it, but, being so yielding, it loses its form
all the more quickly; for the material, unequal to great strain,
accepts their efforts but fails them in use.
So they look for something harder; and yet even here the gold wins favor,
in that it taught them that a rigid metal is more useful.
Next they turn to silver, nearest in beauty and second in its vein,
which, firmer than the soft gold,
better endures service. But bronze is stronger,
though less splendid. Soon, with bronze as teacher,
use passed over to hard steel, and there it stayed.
Perhaps our lyre could also run through in verse all the chances
that opinion imagines to be the supreme craftsmen of the arts:
how, opened up by a silent heat,
the richest earth, its clods baked through,
stirred itself to bear varied offspring, which, with the rain as husband,
the teeming fields released through crumbling passages,
so that their swelling folds crackled and a tall harvest
rose up and trembled, billowing with stirring ears of grain,
that the new settler might learn the look of a cultivated crop;
and how, running from every side to such rich plunder,
the race of birds and beasts and the dark troop
of the smaller throng, thrusting the seeds into their bodies as richer fodder,
impressed on human life foods friendly to it,
of a matter closer to its own, and every task that followed,
which the care of teachable study took up;
how reflection, always drawn from examples as its teachers,
produced the work of art. But the Father's bountiful glory
cries out against these falsehoods: "Let use claim nothing here for itself,
nor powerless chance: it was I who granted my creatures to know
what things are good, together with the light, and willed that the lesser world
should come to know by a sacred sense whatever the greater holds,
and to know me through these things." And would that the mind of man had remained unimpaired,
as it was given to him, and liable to no fault!
Then neither the appearances of things nor their bodies,
nor the measure of the stars, nor the number of the sands, nor their mass
would have deceived it. But over what vast spaces the earth
stretches along with the great deep, what is the measure of the whole
finished mass, what voiced melody of harmony resounds from the motion
of the sevenfold axis — these are now learned by practice
and acquired by constant study, and what remains innate
is thought to be art. Nor does man, dulled by the cloud of evils,
perceive that whatever things he believes he is learning for the first time,
each of us is recognizing again. Let him hold fast to this, then, as the furthest
boundary of truth. When Adam had been driven from the august seats,
he performed no other duty before the one worthy of a husband,
and bestowed loves unknown before upon his children.
Amid so many cares, he who took pleasure in bringing forth
found it sweet to live. He who proved life sweet
lived with God as his guide; nor did his nurslings lack
whatever would furnish life or equip them with the use of things.
And now a house full of children had brought wonderful comfort
to the untaught pair, and in the tender hearts of the parents
a care multiplied lightened their heavy labors,
and now there was hope of delighting in helpers of their own
in the work of the farm. Of these, Cain, the eldest,
turned the rich fields with hard hoes;
but Abel, most worthy to delight in a living gain,
on bare hills or with the growth of the dry plain
fed harmless sheep, and his parents with their milk.
After the joys of the long-awaited produce had satisfied them
and they were amazed to see their hopes surrounded by sacred favor,
justice prompted their minds to dedicate the first offerings of their labors
to God. The elder loads the sacred altars
with new fruits; the younger offers more acceptably a snow-white lamb —
the first figure of priests, soon to be his brother's victim,
an impious one, but even then marked with the sign and token
of a holy victim to come. For when Cain noticed that his brother's
sacrifice had been accepted, while no nod of favor was given to him
as he offered his crops — whether because he had first picked out
the vowed foods for himself and defiled them, or because to Him who sees
all time at once, the man who will one day be guilty is guilty already
in his mind — he drank (dreadful!) the poison from that same spring
from which the serpent and the mother had drunk, and his brother, who did not know
to beware, he cuts down and slaughters in savage murder.
Alas, the crime! What will raging lust not drive the wretched to,
what will fresh anger, old hatred, and the wicked
rivalries in crime that harass the nations not compel, if so great
a crime was committed by one who resented that his brother
was holier than he! Now the parents' guilt is as nothing.
And lest anyone think there is still some complaint left,
at least against the serpent, for the fact that we die: before that,
we began to be killed. Oh, how much the first offspring
added to the crime! Death, brought into the world under the name of punishment,
is scarcely worth mentioning: impiety
made it a new crime. The parents will pay for their sins
by death alone; you will pay the penalty discharged in death
and a penalty for death as well, worse than the accursed serpent.
For he urged death but did not inflict it; but you
will be the first author of murder. You the public enemy,
you the private robber follows; because of you, armed men will punish crimes
with spears, with swords and avenging steel.
Every crime serves in your army, and the fact that peoples to come
will perish less by the death ordained than by slaughter
comes back in sum to you. Nor is this example
wholly unprofitable for morals, that human blood first began
to be shed with a brother's blood, so that
whoever is shown by such a crime to have renewed
the sin against a brother may feel he has committed an equal crime, since reason teaches
that every death of a man not carried off by the original lot
is the murder of a brother. Yet, though he was then dripping with such slaughter,
God does not disdain him — so great is his mercy — but deems him worthy
to be spoken to, and when he denies the deed
he rebukes him, and punishes him lightly for so great a crime,
seeking the measure of the penalty from a part of the deed:
since, though forewarned, he had not feared to commit the dreadful crime,
he should tremble; the fear he would not have as a merit
should become his punishment; what his mind, refusing to take it in,
had thought light, his shaken limbs would prove heavy;
and with his mind struck — that deep torturer by which
every crime avenges itself — the horror of the crime would also break
his body and pass violently into all his limbs,
and his limbs, shaken, would be whirled about in headlong spinning:
as when water enclosed in a basin's rim, with the light struck back from it,
breaks the rays it has caught, a shifting gleam climbs the halls
and, ranging over everything, is nowhere and everywhere;
and as it trembles, a line woven little by little of dim and flashing light
glimmers endlessly amid the blue shadow.
This was not the trembling that cold moisture
inflicts on tightened sinews, when it so stiffens those it fills
with half a death that they cannot lose their life entirely,
but the kind that God's anger stirs, when a power the conscience knows
subdues the mind and hearts are tortured by a sane madness.
[?] Yet what is such a sentence, and how many-sided? It is altogether
vengeance (now) for the murder of the slain, a most just penalty
for the savage culprit, a terror set before the nation and the people to come
as an example, a present cleansing of guilt,
and, as it promised, a sign that guarded his life,
that no one should kill him and strive to destroy with the sword
one whom he sees has paid his penalty. Nor is this
punishment enough: [?] mingling severity with mildness,
he sends him far away and banishes him to vast regions.
This too has its benefit: that he should not defile the fields of the godly;
that his punishment should not stand as a witness proving to peoples yet to be created
that such a crime could be committed; that the condemned race should never mingle with them
nor ever approach the grieving parents —
the condemned race — nor forever heap bitter griefs on the good;
and that the brothers' unlike cases should not torment the bereaved
with grief, the one because their eyes look for him,
the other because they see him, so that they would have to mourn
even this, that he survives. The death of a son, whatever he is like,
is the greatest evil; but where the crime is so great, those visited with such
punishment are, before any judge whatever, more wretchedly
lost while still alive. And what of the fact that it suited him better,
condemned as he was, to depart far from his father's lands,
since he prefers solitude, and it is a heavier punishment to be seen
among the happy and those blessed with a pure mind?
One who is to live on after punishment and the shame of his deed
is spared by exile. Then the fact that a faithful wife is given as companion
to the culprit, and that God's gift does not forsake the condemned,
becomes a sure hope. See, a woman is given to soothe the cares
of his sick heart, to steady with her embrace the broken man
when his body shook, and, liable to no fault,
by her prayers to God alone and by worshiping with a pure mind,
to draw down whatever would be enough for the two of them.
O good Majesty, what may we not hope for!
You yourself supply hidden paths to pardon and the means
by which you may help the guilty man, whom with offspring following
you increase and multiply through a thousand names of descendants,
and soon you set him up as king of his own people, from being
its first father. For he was the first to teach how to gird cities with walls,
which no one can do unless a populace has been gathered.
And by confessing in fear what he deserved, he roused an avenger
from the race of his own kin [?], and taught that he would perish
while he feared being killed; and perhaps, expiated by that slaying,
he washed away his offense, since he paid it back by a like death;
and death itself is gain, since it became the punishment of his crime.
Meanwhile Eve, with child again, had made up to her grieving husband
for the first loss with a holy pledge,
and had once more given the parent cares and hopes.
The boy's name was Seth, whom, with favoring will,
the Almighty granted to fill Abel's place, his virtues aided from on high,
a gift which the joy of the glad father
did not keep silent, and which the line that followed confirmed.
For from this man's seed sprang Enos,
who, chosen as the first priest for his quiet virtue,
hoped to be able to call upon God with pious prayers and by his true name,
and was found worthy; and he instructed the people who followed him
to keep the worship of the eternal Father
and to use his sacred help wherever life required it.
And the Almighty, because they extolled him, acknowledging his majesty,
gave them both understanding and merit, and for many years
allowed the penalty of the ancient crime to be postponed,
so much so that Enoch, mighty in every virtue,
from the line of those whom that kindly stock contains,
was restored to his fatherland's seats and the blessed world,
and lives still, and already possesses the realms of the life to come.
For when the world was newly tilled and still lacking [?],
there was a contest among the living as to who would draw out his years beyond nine hundred
and fill up the thousand, the tenth hundred cut short —
such was the rivalry of the living. But after crimes
had infected their minds, and the fathers' guilt was born again in the following stock,
and each offspring, worse than its elder,
kept adding to vice whatever the heir might surpass it with,
shortness of life came to the rescue, since the one limit
on the growth of wickedness was the one that ended the light of life.
For when the youth of the better blood, joined to the Cainites
in profane marriages, had condemned itself,
deserted by sacred favor it fell into every kind of crime
and, laid open, let the enemy in through his snares,
while God spoke thus: "Not forever shall our
spirit abide in these peoples, nor shall their guilty life put off
the time appointed for a late death beyond twice six times ten
years, since, in following earthly things,
they have more of the flesh than of the mind." So whether the stern
sentence of the kindly judge broke nature,
so as to show that every guilty man has more of the brute mother
from which he was born, or whether, after the first gift
that it had given to the servants it created by sacred power,
the generous grace of the divine faculty — so as to show that it
had passed from the whole man to the body alone —
was transmitted through the fathers' sins: suddenly there were born
monstrous men, giants of towering bulk of limb,
savage and swollen in mind. As much power as dire spirits
had at hand through such bodies, and as much as they must needs desire,
crushed by unjust servitude to so great a bulk,
so they thought nothing forbidden too profane to violate,
and nothing lawful was dear to them; their lust, inflamed by what was forbidden,
burned more fiercely, and it was not beauty but crime that set the price
on what they sought. No nights without blood,
no days without slaughter; it was sweet to eat their meals amid a kinsman's
tears, and to outrage their very kinsmen by making them food,
unmindful of the law of fellowship, of mankind and of themselves,
of sacred affection, of their own mothers and fathers,
and of the author of heaven; and so far into the worst of crimes
had they advanced that God regretted having formed all the creatures
to which he had given life and light, and, because of the guilty, he preferred
to sweep away even souls free from crime
rather than not drown the lands in a headlong sea,
the world returning once more to its ancient (shape).
[?] faithful
had now for five hundred years led a life free of crime
and had proved himself, living under the law that had been laid down.
To him God, disclosing holy secrets, reveals them thus:
"Since the lands are given over to vice and men are prone to crime,
with virtue cast aside, preparing to remedy evils by an end
of things, I have resolved — since I foresee that to punish every fault
would be cruel, and that it is milder to blot out the guilty —
to drown the lands once more by bringing in the sea,
so that, as it rushes in and covers all, and subsides at my command,
it may wash the polluted world with its headlong flood
and roll up the entangled men, and whatever was bidden to live
for the sake of men, in the ruin of the swollen deep.
But since you alone, to whom our will is dear,
spending a devoted life under sacred laws,
have always stood against this with better merit,
I will so temper the rigor of my decrees
that, when the wicked have paid their just due, the mortal race
may begin anew more worthily from you, and the peoples
who will enjoy our light may count you as their first father.
So let an ark be prepared for you, built of squared beams,
stretching three hundred cubits in length,
fifty in breadth, and rising in height
only thirty; through [?]
[?] let it be finished, narrowing to a single point
at the top. But let a door be left in its side, through which [?]
let the assembled structure rise to a peak beneath a sloping roof.
Then let hot bitumen, breathing through the absorbent framework,
search out the fine cracks and coat them on every side,
spread like a skin. After that, let the greatest labour call you
inside: let the sides be joined on either hand
to huge posts, and the parts of the finished stalls be laid down;
and when a double floor has divided the space into three,
let the living creatures be separated thus into their own nests,
so that they do not defile their kind by mixing, or fight when thrown together,
or confuse their foods, of which it is fitting for you to lay up
only the supply; for that, once it is shared out, it should not fail
those taken in is my task to ensure." With a faithful mind
he received these words — for God himself, supplying mind and senses,
gave his servant the will and the power for whatever he commanded —
and with his sons and a crowd of gathered
people he set about laying low with iron the dense forests born for this purpose.
The groves let in the rays of light, the plain is relieved of shadow,
the valleys are stripped of oaks as old as themselves,
and the woods that would enfold the likeness of a smaller world.
But though the whole of the work begun had been hurried on
with so much labour, it was put off for a hundred years,
so that the peoples might repent of their crime and strive against the wrath.
O wretched beyond measure, whom the delay of so just a punishment
makes all the more guilty: now they will be punished
not only for their crime, though they had ample means of seeking pardon,
but they will be punished for this too, that so many will go down to dread Tartarus
within the span of time granted them, though God
bears witness that he would rather spare all. Now the great mass was complete,
and there stood, woven together in a capacious framework of sides,
the help which the Father himself had prepared as the last resort
for your shipwreck, O Nature, and he was setting the cause in motion,
when God from high Olympus deigned to warn his servant
Noah by his voice that the final hour was now at hand
to hide himself in the refuge, and to snatch the mother, his sons and their wives
from the impending destruction and the darkness of death
into a life-giving prison, and with him all the living creatures
that the earth nourishes as its own and the air upholds though not its own:
seven of each sex of those which God approved as clean,
two by two in pairs, but of the unclean kind one of each sex.
There is no delay: whatever is born, unknown to us, beneath the curved vault of heaven
in the various regions of the world,
whatever the East marvels at, whatever the pale Iberian shudders at,
whatever rages on the hot sands of southern Libya,
whatever cleaves the Hyperborean nights with wondrous light,
rushes together in fear and plunges into the open ark.
You would think they had sensed the flood; for since God the Maker
gives sense to brute creatures, by which he bears witness to himself before his nurslings,
the beasts have more reason, for, moved by the divine will,
they know nothing of themselves. So, as soon as God commands
the ark, heavy with every seed of life, to be shut,
night rushes in, sudden darkness veils the sky,
and the storm-cloud, falling as the air pours out, strikes the earth
headlong, like a passing shower, yet set to hold its course;
it rages and storms over the whole world alike
just as it does in one region, when, stirred by a swift whirlwind,
a tempest follows the savage fires of lightning or announces them,
and heaven and earth echo back the thunder.
Nor is the rain that streams from the clouds enough for the destruction:
the ancient waters are loosed, and now, with the heavens opened,
the sky rains into the emptied clouds; the vapour that supplies the rivers,
stretching through the inmost parts of the earth, fills them
and opens new springs as great as torrents.
And while all that the sky, that the earth spews up, that the clouds pour down,
rushes together, mingled in a single flood,
it engulfs the drowned fields together with their tillers,
and flocks trapped in their stalls; it overwhelms cities
with their citizens: amid the waters whole peoples perished in the ruins.
No face of things remains; the flood covers everything,
and the rivers, as they swell, lose their names,
and soon their courses too. The ocean, never sated
by any rivers, now feels the waters rushing in
in so vast a mass; grown greater by the swollen flood, it drives them back
and forces them, as they return, to rise into a heap,
until, as the deep lifts its surge and the shores shrink
on every side, the flood joins itself at the highest circuit
and the seas run together over the overwhelmed lands.
And now the ark was borne along fifteen cubits
higher than everything; for this was the height by which the flood
exceeded the highest mountains, when for forty days
there had been the fury of a single [?] rain and one unbroken night.
After a hundred and fifty days, when the air was clear
and the sea still kept the same level and measure,
the Almighty, pitying those shut inside, ordered the great sea
to recede little by little, whether he wished to spare all the lands
which, fleeing headlong, it could have overturned,
or those shut inside, whom the wave, slipping back gently
as it withdrew, might set down more safely on a firm seat.
At last a mountain [?], level on its broad summit,
received the burden it was to [?] carry. Now the highest ridges
could be seen and could break the level waves with their crags,
and, as the sea gradually settled, the woods
began to break through, and the hidden hills slowly to rise.
And now the black scout sent out from the opened ark
had shown that the air was calm, and, having found prey,
was detained there; but that they must still wait in their chamber and enclosure
the weary dove reports, which, sent out again, brings back
a small offering of the peace-bearing fruit of the olive.
At this sign, with praise of the great Father,
there arises among those shut inside such weeping, by which they reveal [?] their joy,
as great as when, while a cruel victor
assails the walls, sudden help happens to reach
the besieged; as great as when a sentence sent by a merciful judge
restores the condemned to life once more;
as great as when life returns to a body thought dead,
amid the tears and the joy of the mourners — such was the weeping.
After the scout, sent out a third time, announced that the fields lay open
by the very fact that, captivated by the recovered lands,
she did not return, they grew weary of enduring their idle hiding place,
the nearer was their hope of breathing under the open sky
and of feeding their released souls on the sense of the heavens.
But no one may go out onto the shores of light,
just as no one may be born and come beneath the sky and the day,
unless God calls; and he with his own voice
commanded the trembling Noah to leave the sacred enclosure
with his faithful wife, his sons and their chaste wives,
and to give the land anew to husbandmen led out once more,
together with all the creatures which, preserved alike for future offspring,
the mighty Craftsman had formed for human use.
Once the door was opened, these rushed out: some sought the air on their wings,
some the glades and woods, some, plunging into caves,
burrowed into the earth's wide hollows, some, free on the dry plains,
leapt for joy and frolicked like springtime in the open meadow.
But their lord, who had received the realm of a second world,
Noah, rejoicing, took in everything with his eyes and his capacious mind,
and could not sate his soul however much he filled it,
and, swiftly surveying everything with eager gaze,
marvelled at it all as new. Brighter than at its familiar rising
and redder was the sun; the glad face of the sky smiled
with a greater calm, and the fields once despaired of grew green
with new growth. But still the image of so great a ruin,
never to be forgotten, hovered before his eyes:
what they had suffered among the waters, and what, by a sacred gift,
they had not suffered, when the sea roared with savage blows
and the ark scorned the storms that dashed against it;
and with his family he considered how widely the holy bounty
of the supreme Father had plainly poured itself around them,
and he taught them, astonished as they were and eager to learn the truth,
whence food had sufficed for so many through a whole year,
and what drink; for this much is certain: even if everything else needed for life
had been at hand, those shut inside, while the ark was tossed about,
could have died of thirst among the waters, had not the Ruler of Olympus
sustained them, hidden away deep within and no longer fearing any extremity,
by the same nod with which he founded all things.
He filled with strength souls that would have perished in the prison of the long night,
taking from them their longing for the light;
he, so that they could endure so idle a rest,
poured into them a placid love of sluggish torpor;
he is mighty, who, if he pleases, has the right with stern power
swiftly to make the wicked burn though plunged beneath an icy flood,
and the good feel cold though carried
into the flames to come; who in a short time,
just as he has now taught the peoples that they can be killed in this way,
will himself teach the peoples that in this way, by water, they can be born again.
BOOK THREE.
Bearing such thoughts in mind and discerning the ages to come,
Noah resolved not to undertake any mortal task
before he had rendered to God the ancient rites and his thanks.
Altars rise of snow-white stone:
since no building enclosed them with its walls,
the world, spread out on every side beneath the curved path of heaven,
was their temple. Victims came in haste, from every group of seven,
from the flocks which the soft air upholds,
which the earth brings forth … [?]
… [?] are strewn, from the East
or the forests of the Arabs. Fire sent down from Olympus
He offers fragrant honours, which the fire's tresses consume,
and the burnt offerings breathe an ambrosial vapour up to God.
He, gentle and ever good, accepting in return for our gift
whatever he receives, and rejoicing in the dutiful
services of godly men, whose use he does not need
but by which he might redeem us, speaks thus with tranquil majesty:
“Although it was a slight vengeance, for so great a cause,
to have condemned with avenging rains and a soft flood
those guilty of so many crimes, and to have renewed the earth,
the dwelling of the wicked, with the outpoured deep instead,
yet, though offended, we shall not strike with such a lash
the mortal race any further, even though I see that human minds
and profane nations will fall again through every kind of wickedness,
through their former crimes.
For since mortals will never cease to commit
what deserves punishment, it befits us to cease always repaying
what their deserts have earned. Grow joyfully [?], my nurslings,
grow without fear, and fill the fields with fruitful offspring,
and spread new herds across all the lands.
The elements will keep their turns, and through all days
the due harvest will be returned to its own seeds.
The work of the world will run on, balanced in its warring seasons:
winter will contend with summer, and, weighing the seasons
of spring and autumn, the fleeting year will roll round again.
And you, to whom we have entrusted rule over the solid globe,
whom every race of living things fears and feels as its masters,
we command you to keep this point of the law and, bound
by the precepts of strict justice, always to remember it:
among all the kinds of creatures which, moving their limbs freely
by the life within them, we now grant a second time for your use,
let no one make pallid flesh, still mingled with its blood,
into foul food; for that crime the sentence of a stern
judgment will one day punish no less than if
some savage were to drain human blood with the sword —
blood which I shall always demand back as avenger, and require so strictly
that not only the one endowed with reason shall pay me
the penalty, but the brute beasts too: let human blood
be equally sacred to all that enjoy our light.
And let there be signs by which, while the sky shines, we may bear witness
that the waters of the flood have been withdrawn: for when, in the dense air,
the light moisture hangs suspended in thin mists
and the cloud is already gathering black waters into its hollows,
I shall pour forth my rays, and with its topmost circuit
the curved image of the sun will adorn for me a beautiful bow,
painting the vault of heaven, so that, warming it with light,
it may dry up the rains and scatter the showers into the air,
so far that the second age of the world may take
this sign as a foretaste of the punishment to come,
since it has more of glowing fire and now less of rain.”
Awed by such commands, at which all things tremble,
and quickened by the gracious promises, in which all things rejoice,
Noah and his sons together, whose span of life was sturdier,
vie with one another in breaking with their mattocks the fields,
glad with mud and sweet moisture, and wed the land with seed.
Already in spring the grass, spread thickly far across the plains,
turning from stalks of food to grain with its milk congealed,
returns a manifold harvest with heaped-up interest;
and the new vineyard, its branches now heavy-laden, runs riot
with rich fruit, which it swells with sweet nectar
and brings to birth, and cups of drink are born from hard wood.
It happened that while Noah was joyfully celebrating the Lord's honours,
indulging in feasting and sipping sweet cups,
he felt the power of the living liquor, and, overcome
by heavy sleep, laid his limbs carelessly on his faithful couch;
and at the same time his garment, rolled back, uncovered the secret parts
of his body, and stirred your laughter, Ham, worst of sons —
the very fount and origin of you — and you set about involving your brothers
in the stain of your guilt, Shem first and Japheth the eldest.
Learn what is demanded by what [?] with a guffaw
you alone: the better judgment of your brothers
thinks it an occasion for duty; for, seizing a covering
and holding it behind their backs, stepping slowly backward,
with faces turned away they covered their father's shame with their hands,
and each snatched from the other the prize of piety
set between them. For after Noah's heart, freed from sleep,
recovered the messages of divine perception,
he repaid his sons' deserts with this reward:
