“Ham, accursed, you who were faltering in duty to your parent,
shall be the slave of your brothers; you, the eldest born,
Shem, blessed by holy God, shall live; and your younger brother
the Lord will spread with abundant seed across the wide world,
until his numerous offspring establish a dwelling
even in his brother's houses and, mingled with the neighbouring peoples,
fill the adjoining cities and those it will itself build.”
Having said this, the old man, when he had already run through
a thousand years less fifty, which the full sum lacked,
his heart aware of what was to come, was released in death;
he departed and left this world and its cares to his sons.
For it was granted to those free of guilt and far from vice,
even after the sin that is atoned for by the first death,
when the Spirit of God had wholly filled the sanctuary
of a chosen mind and had watered a friendly heart,
to know all things at once and to behold them as if set before their eyes:
what fleeting time has snatched away, what is, and what the age
will one day bring, to be reaped by descendants yet to come,
and whatever, once conceived, is poured out for the varied uses of men
by the heavy earth, the liquid sea, the quickening air,
and what greedy fire too brings forth from its abundant fuel.
But after the condemned race had lost so great a gift,
and nothing remained to the wretched except that they had known
the secrets of their ancestors, each one, mindful, recalled
within himself the teachings of his parents and, turning everything over —
what suited what, in what ways, in what part of nature they would help —
[resolved] to store them up in this, in the once-fixed elements of speech
or in signs, committing words to solid shape.
From this the arts took their origin; writing, preserving
the inventions of the ancients, sent them down to slow descendants,
and, mingling the discoveries of the new with the studies of the old,
gave hope to the bewildered; and the headlong quest for the future
dragged those stirred by vain desire into what is forbidden:
whether he gave to the world — which some, in fallen error,
have called a bodily god — what the almighty Creator alone
possessed, and scattered through all the members
of things moving signs, messengers of the age to come,
so that throughout the whole fabric he might bear witness to himself
before his nurslings, and the image of the mind might ever confess its author,
and it might be plainly set forth in things what the bountiful ruler
can bestow on peoples, what he can take away,
and what and when he forbids his servants, for whom the kingdoms of heaven are prepared,
to know — a truth which the agate as witness,
the gem of Pyrrhus, proves, with the Muses and Apollo enclosed in it,
brought forth together with the world — what should we not believe
God has signified through all things, when he even exposed the world's lies
in advance and marked out what would later be feigned?
Or whether rather the simple motion of the world brings all things about;
or whether the grim inventor of death, not suffering
the material apt for deceit to lie idle, subjected all things
to his malignant will, so as to bring fate upon the world.
For while he counts the courses and the various returns
of the stars and delights in the wondrous distinctions of the sky,
he has thus fixed for himself set times of fickle favour
and a ready power and limits for doing harm,
producing varied effects at various conjunctions,
so as to cast odium on the stars and lay crimes to the charge
of holy heaven and the stars that adorn the world,
while he pretends to the peoples that whatever he himself does was foretold.
Hence the art of reading how the entrails quiver, how the wing flashes,
what the lightning bolts signal as messengers when the clouds are dashed together.
For since, having grasped with shrewd study all headlong motions
and chances, the public enemy remembers
what [?] renders, he persuaded the peoples
to think the inventions of a false poison divine.
In just the same way, among the Ethiopians, whose kingdoms belong to dogs,
liberty is ruled by tyrants: when a judgment suited to definite matters
is sought from the motion of an unknowing body,
and they take chance for commands. Nor are these signs lesser
which opinion claims for itself with strong conviction;
for Galba's Fortune refutes the gem of Pyrrhus:
he who could fashion a statue over so many years
can also counterfeit a stone. Using these frauds,
he mocked those captivated by a passion to know the future,
and then, as fear spurred them on to overcome fate,
he brought upon those anxious in their zeal the crime of the magic art,
so that they might worship him instead and on dedicated altars
offer impious incense, once the throng had been betrayed by its parent.
And soon Nimrod, born of an unsound stock,
a giant in bulk and in mind, master of the court of Babylon,
capturing the minds of the Persians, an unjust hunter,
led them away from the rites of the true Lord to the worship of fire.
Nor did he alone mock the cares of men too eager
with such shrewd art — he, the head of crimes, the world's accused and his own enemy —
but he rushed into their very minds
and descended deep into all their senses,
and soon into their affections too. For when a father's only child
had dragged with him into bitter death the hope of his family,
the unhappy father, prolonging his tears night and day
and drawing out his complaints in dull lamentation,
while he raged and sought his stolen son in every single thing,
and clung to the sweet relics of his boyish years,
or, devoted beyond death, consoled his grief with an image,
so fed the love that longing had inflamed
that, setting up the whole figure in Parian marble,
he believed in his madness that it lived with feeling shut inside it
and heard his laments; and on dedicated altars
he transferred the worship of the supreme Creator to shades.
This man surpasses all the guilty in gravity, even that
very [?] teacher of crimes who founded the magic arts.
The one is openly guilty through frenzy and a profane mind,
the other does harm through piety. This crime defiles the more
because it has the appearance of virtue; for at once all
the nations embraced this crime, endlessly offering
sacrifices to the spirits of the dead — as the Alans still attest —
and each held their dear parents in place of their gods,
and afterwards their kings as well; under whose names lying
Greece, labouring to slip falsehoods in among truths,
added obscure shadows with empty explanations,
excusing tombs and names laid away in graves,
until madness stretched out through every form
and fashioned gods out of the meanest things and shameful members:
for at such shrines there stood by,
fostering errors and stirring up oracles,
the inventor of death, in wondrous parts of the world,
using for his snares either fire or a hot spring
or caves. With winds made talkative by the earth's breathing
he deceived men first as Themis; afterwards, as false Apollo,
he imposed on the peoples; and then, forced to change his seat,
having become the physician of the Leuci, and now crossing the fields of Gaul
as a fugitive, with harmful fraud he stirs up
the German nations and deceives barbarian hearts.
But I return to the main thread from which I digressed, to that
line of the forefathers. When Noah's offspring, multiplied by begetting,
had filled all the lands of the East
and saw the fields of Shinar grow narrow and scant,
the young men, who were to be scattered through the various parts of the world,
broke out into these mournful complaints in the saddest words:
“Alas, how uncertain is the state of life that carries men
from the order once begun, and how prosperity cheats the faith once pledged
through its shifting courses, so that the sum of the prayer we sought
turns to the contrary! Now we — if it is right to say so —
regret that the throng of descendants, hoped for in our fathers' prayers,
has grown so numerous; for the band we have begotten must be scattered
through the world in exile: perishing to its kin
and losing them in turn — which is sharper still to grief —
it repays its own with a living death; and we wretches are condemned
to a sad end, since, with old age hastening on,
whereas the former age reached ten hundred years,
we, worn out, scarcely now attain three hundred,
lest, exiled from our homeland, we give our bare and nameless limbs
to be buried here and there in unknown graves.
Come then, young men, while our numbers supply the strength,
[make] something that can outlive you and know no harsh end:
stretch out an everlasting fame by your deeds.
Let us found a city, and under its name let us raise a tower
so high that it bursts through the stars that paint the world
and the vaults of lofty Olympus,
so that posterity, when we have left these lands,
may think we have migrated to heaven.” So roused, the young men
scorn rocks and whatever is hewn from a quarried mountain:
from the bowels of the subdued earth they bind moulded
bricks with fire, and prefer to owe the material
of the work to come to their own labour.
Bitumen laid between binds it fast on either side,
so that the walls set all around look like solid rock.
Now the tower rises in haste, now with its peak it leaps
above the clouds and enjoys the nearer calm of heaven,
when the Father begins to speak thus to the partners of his kingdom:
“Behold, what would this earthly phalanx in its fury not break open,
which believes that with a structure raised by mortal hands it can reach
the lofty poles and carry it up to our heaven?
No one clothed in an earthly body ascends to heaven
except he who has come down from high heaven.
But since — they are one people, with one and the same way of speaking —
the throng has followed with eager assent those who urged what is wrong,
and has not weighed what right permits, daring
heights which nature of itself forbade to be reached,
let them bear, with no further punishment, the loss of so vain a labour.
Yet so that they may know that what was impossible was also forbidden,
let us now go down and confound their hearts, swollen with proud
agreement, with the sounds of diverse speech,
so that the sin the populace committed in concord toward crime
may be condemned by the better discord of a confused tongue.”
He spoke, and upon them, intent on the work and raising the mass,
forgetfulness first stole into their stunned minds,
and the full command of an unknown tongue came upon them.
As zeal for the work slackens, the overseers rebuke
their loitering comrades; but no one answers
words not understood, and if anyone tries to open his mouth,
he hisses, or pants with the rumble of broken speech,
or shrieks and mimics threats with a shrill groan.
So the baffled band abandons the vain labour
undertaken with perverse intent: now no one follows his kinsman,
no one his father: each joins to himself whomever he understands
and gathers him close: all kinship has perished;
language makes the nation: they are scattered in matched companies
and make for lands set apart under different stars.
Just so the birds across the soft levels of the plain,
which a carefree day has coaxed to wander in mingled flocks
and seek their food, when night draws near
and they make for their leafy roofs, at once in a gathering throng
each follows its own kind, and in swift flight
they mingle wherever like colour or like voice has led them:
so then the one people split itself into parts,
and each kind became a race, and in far-distant lands
they settle and fill the world with nations.
And yet this, though it is the fitting punishment of the guilty,
is not without a holy gift; for although this was a just
vengeance — that those whom reverence for heaven did not touch,
which is the proper seat of the Father of the world and of all things,
should not know one another — such a punishment bestows more
on the guilty nurslings: it prevents what the persuasion to sin
of a few had brought in from contaminating all again
and making wickedness common; it prevents bloody wars
and death summoned upon peoples by rabid fury
from being endless, and keeps citizens and nurslings driven out from grieving
to leave their kin. For lest the exiled throng should ever
long for its own, it must even hate them of its own accord:
and so diverse speech brings this about, that no one
should wish to remember his own. Yet the sound of the Hebrew
tongue and the ancient speech remained among those
who, free of guilt, were the blameless part
of the sons whom Shem begot, whom a father's holy
care sustains and reverence for the true God touches.
But after a madness stirred up throughout the whole world —
to say nothing of the abominable crime of the magical monster —
drove the mortal race onto tree-trunks and stones, and even onto
hollow forms wrought by the art of hard metal, and figures void of light,
and broke minds that gazed on things above
and bound them over to inert earth,
the contagion of that foul stain engulfed these too.
Just so, roused from the burning lands of the Ethiopians,
clouds of disease, along the corrupted pathway of the sky,
wrapped the hollows in a greedy, conquering plague,
when whoever groaned, struck by the swift thunderbolt of death,
at once fell himself; whoever saw another falling
fell too; and everywhere the dire pestilence strewed heaped corpses
across the plains and finished off the war:
so then error, embracing all in the headlong mass of its fury,
came back and seized even those it had passed over,
until the line, descending by successive steps,
to which Shem, its fount and origin, had given a noble birth,
came down to Terah, who, leaving the chief seat
of the Chaldean race with the whole stock of his kin,
and seeking another city, new customs and a new home,
settled at last as a newcomer in Assyrian Haran.
And when he had completed two hundred and five years,
he passed away in the manner of his fathers. But his son Abram,
a man worthy of heaven, from the very threshold of life
worshipping the true God in his mind, had turned away
from the rites of the gentiles. When, after his father's death,
he was at last free to follow God's commands without deceit,
the Lord deigned to approach his servant with these instructions:
“Since in all the world we have found you alone
in whom sincere faith and reverence for us take delight,
leave far behind your ancestral home, the guilty lands
and your polluted house: your whole kindred is profane
and must be shunned by you. Into the fields of a better land
you shall come with me as your guide, lest you be part of a wicked nation,
you who can be the head of a holy one. Then I shall appoint sacred rites
to remain yours, blessed one, and I shall make your name
great among all peoples, repaying every good
or evil according to the deserts of those whose differing will
has been shown toward you, through whom a blessing poured out
shall be spread to all the tribes and to a reborn age.”
He spoke, and gave him a mind with which to serve his commands
and trust the holy promises. No delay holds him back:
with flocks of various kinds and his father's servants,
with his faithful wife, and with the son of his dear brother,
whose name was Lot, setting out on a straight course
he takes a road unknown to him. The softest fields
offer glad paths, and the air, smiling sweetly with favouring south winds,
is troubled by no disturbance,
until he entered Canaan, the land of the peoples Ham begot,
and the richest countryside of Shechem.
When he heard from God's voice that this was granted to him
and to his future offspring, he raises devoted altars,
and, a new worshipper, renewing the ancient honours, increases them.
From there he makes for Bethlehem, a place chosen and hallowed
by the lodging of the blessed man, which surpassed all lands
in its lofty merits whenever — though it must be named in second place
after the heavenly seat —
it seemed the worthier, since it was to receive the pledge of God,
sent forth into the world by the law of salvation and made ready while the world marvelled,
and to send man back to the stars.
Here too father Abram raises solemn altars
and sets up dwellings in the new fields, which he would have to leave.
For, forced again by famine to change his home,
he breaks camp and drives with him his whole household, servants and flocks,
and, paying fair exchange for goods,
enters Egypt. But his beautiful wife is protected
under the name of sister, lest raging lust spur barbarian hearts
to murder the holy guest.
Soon, indeed, Pharaoh, led on by the vision of her radiant beauty,
burns with desire and prepares a marriage and a compact bound by fixed
law; but terror, steeped in utter dread,
falls upon him and shakes his wicked heart with sudden turmoil,
black horror affrights his mind and grips his limbs,
so that the king of a sacrilegious nation
felt that God had condemned such grim desires — God who indeed
had inspired such counsel in his servants, so that the barbarian foe
would recognize that Abram was safer then as Sarah's husband,
having learned that not with impunity would he attack with profane
sword a man whom it was not lawful even to rob of his wife.
Of his own accord, then, he restores her to her husband, defiled by no stain,
confesses his fault, and sends him back safe under a large
escort and laden with much produce
to Shechem and his own Bethlehem; and joyfully they work
the fields regained and graze the rich pastures far and wide
with their flocks intermingled. But there were frequent quarrels
among the herdsmen; for the land lay open, marked off
by no boundary for anyone. So, full
of foresight, yet most observant of equal justice,
to settle disputes and remove greedy quarrels,
Abram, being the elder, divides the granted fields.
The younger chose the part where, with sweet waters poured all around,
the Jordan weds the countryside, glides in streams between shady banks
and makes the smooth glades lovely.
Captivated by these, and turning from his uncle's house and its just strictness,
Lot moves to the fields that border Sodom,
while God strengthened Abram's sorrowful heart with this hope,
saying: “Do not grieve that, left by your brother's son,
you have suffered the loss of a holy father's line. A countless multitude
you alone shall be to me, you who shall hold the realms of a people —
those you see with the first sun, those you look out on toward the north,
and those you look back on lying beneath the warm south wind,
and those shut in by the shore of the wide-spread sea.
These I shall grant to you, to your offspring and the peoples of your line
for an everlasting age, living for ever.
So that [?] you may now enjoy these lands far and wide,
rise and first survey on foot, as a guest, the tracts that lie open.”
So he spoke; Abram gladly obeys and, leaving his dwelling,
moves on and comes to Hebron, and beneath the spreading foliage
of the dark oak of Mamre he pitches his tents;
and, a shrewd leader, to add a safeguard to his new camp,
here too he builds solemn altars to the Lord, to worship him.
Meanwhile, amid a great tumult raging all around,
a greedy enemy is at hand, lured by a land
filled with every kind of wealth: the hoof pounds the plains
and rebounds, and the plunderer roams with loosened reins.
Lot, together with the king, bursts out through the opened gates,
and with them a neighbouring band of kings bearing allied arms:
they draw horsemen and foot soldiers with them, the column stretches out,
the lines clash, and alike they strike down and fall.
The invaders had help enough in this, that in preparing to make war
they had already pictured their foes falling suddenly in slaughter;
the defenders were sustained only by the image of a better cause.
But the youth of Sodom, softened by foul luxury,
when the shout was raised again and blazed up into rage,
turn their backs in fear: some make for the walls at a run,
some for the mountains and woods; some, hemmed in by troops,
hold out cowardly hands to grim chains.
As soon as his uncle Abram learned that Lot had been captured,
not with weeping — for what would empty weeping achieve? —
but with dutiful reason he chooses from his whole household
three hundred and eighteen servants, whom he equips with arms,
and follows gradually where the enemy's track betrayed his course,
slow and heavy with plunder; and he takes care to come upon them
in the first night of their rest, when sweet sleep already floods
their languid hearts and binds their weary limbs.
So, when the mad rage of a hungry lion
has burst with a swift leap into the folds of a flock in the glade,
it kills them all with tooth and paw, and its anger postpones
its greedy hunger to devour, while a wondrous patience born of fear
stifles the groans of bitter pain in the stricken beasts:
such was the leader's bearing then. Laying low the people and the kings,
buried in sleep and wine, they slaughter them with silent
wounds. No tumult throws the camp into confusion;
no one perceives a footstep except one whose mind and voice are already fleeing;
no one hears the sound of slaughter except one whom death awakens.
Everything is drenched with blood; the earth, loosened despite the dry, clear weather,
clots with gore, and as the blood slows their steps,
their slippery footing totters on the stained field.
Yet not all of every age are cut down by the sword together:
some are kept as spoil — so great is the moderation of the just
victor — those whom anyone might now lawfully, without wrong,
take captive; the rest shameful flight scattered, and pressing terror
pursued them as far as the fields of Hobah.
But the victor, not at all moved by the glory of so great a triumph,
amid horses and flocks of cattle and people recovered
or captured, and treasures whose greedy weight burdens
vanquished and victors alike — gentle amid such rejoicing,
and pondering in his heart the fortunes of men —
returns with hardly more than a loser's gain, and restores the plunder and the prizes of war
to the peoples and the king who had been despoiled on every side,
showing that he had not fought for himself; yet he offers a tenth
of the plunder wrested from the enemy — which is the true offering —
to Melchizedek, who was then the devoted care of the highest Father,
bearing witness that God had won the victory; and he earned of the future
forewarned, even then to take the mystic offerings of the sacrament to come
into his hands. And when he had set his course toward greater rewards
through the voice of so great a priest invoking every blessing,
the Lord too honored his servant with the gift of his speech:
"Since no plunder has subdued you with its lures
and made you greedy, the price of your faith and the wage of your labors
are stored in full with me, and I will guard you and all that is yours,
to be kept for your heir, whom, born as late offspring
of your own body, you, his loving father, will love far more
than the one you now long for in your heart, in whose place this man of Damascus pleases you,
adopted from your household of servants, while the sweet infancy of a foster child
kindles and stirs a father's feelings
and beguiles the love that hurries after sons.
Look up and see how the vaulted sky glitters with dense light
in the painted night, how the stars are heaped and pressed
upon stars and, set before your eyes, refuse to be numbered:
take this as the pattern of your seed, and from this hold
the form and worth of the stock to come." So he spoke; and Abram
believed, and the bare assent of faith alone
stood in place of virtue, and, adorned as if with the merits of labor,
being reckoned to him, it bestowed the full crown of righteousness.
And so the virtue of holy Abram, so noble here,
shows that it is good to believe in the divine Christ,
who, the living voice of the Father, spoke again to Abram thus:
"I am the almighty Lord, who brought you and yours
out of the Chaldean nation, and at last, freed
from your fathers' vices, settled you in a better land,
so that my people, begotten through you, might dwell in the blessed fields
and spread their line far and wide
once the nations are driven out whom the foul error of their parents
and profane rites long ago made sacrilegious.
But since you hesitate and sin by doubting what you should believe,
take for me a heifer three years old, already grim of brow,
and with her a she-goat of equal years chosen from the gentle flock,
and a ram of the same age, and let them be slain in my honor;
and when a dove joined with a chaste turtledove
has closed the sacrifice and the rite of offering has made the total complete,
let the victim of birds feel the knife no further.
But let the beasts be split down the middle, their bellies opened,
and let the three bodies alone be parted into two halves,
which, divided thus, you will set apart on clean sand,
so that on either side matching limbs may face limbs
in a fourfold double row. Then what you are bidden to hope for
will come of its own accord into view, and you will prove it with your eyes."
He spoke; and Abram, accustomed to serve God's commands gladly,
hastens at once to carry out what he was told.
But when he had laid out the pieces on the ground
in the order commanded, suddenly a black swarm swooped down
of greedy birds, lured by the prey.
Lest they defile the sacred offerings with profane touch,
Abram anxiously keeps guard and looks around on every side.
But when, though he was dazed by so great a task, not even with the setting sun
could the heavy burden of the duty he had taken on overcome him,
behold, black terror, dreadful trembling and sleep came over him,
bearing messages of commands and shaping the ages to come.
He seemed, I believe, to see the Nile hemming in
the peoples of the Hebrew race, and his late descendants,
and to recognize the throngs that would count themselves up to the utmost;
then the fierce uprisings and the camps of his people led out,
the sea crossed on dry foot, the hosts sunk in the deep,
and how an army on land, which had pursued with no fleet at all,
had suffered shipwreck; and then how the whole realm of blessed
Palestine lay open to the returning people.
To him, astonished by such sights, a gracious interpreter
was not lacking: "Learn beforehand of your own and of their offspring,
who, born after you, will grow up in foreign lands
and feel the servile yoke of the Nile's tyrant;
and when they have fulfilled four hundred years in harsh
slavery, I will rescue them and take vengeance on their unjust masters,
and restore them to the lands girded with gentle streams by
the Nile and the Euphrates, but only when the sins of the guilty
Amorite race and of the people holding these realms
have filled up the full measure of crimes and they are worthy to be driven
from their ancestral homes. But you, before then,
departing happy at the long-lived limit of life,
praised by your sons, in peace and by my gift,
will pass to your holy forefathers." So he spoke; and when
night was already drawing thick shadows over the earth,
he gave a sign from a lofty mountain; for a furnace flashed out suddenly
with bright fire and twisted its trailing tail downward
and sought the divided pieces, and the flame, borne into the prepared space between,
touched them in its headlong course and consecrated them.
Not otherwise do torches, darting their bodies through thick air,
fly slantwise through the void and billow, flashing
with nocturnal splendor; so a deceptive star trails
its red hair, and clouds shaken by the winds
shake loose a downward fire to lash the earth.
Meanwhile, certain of the kingdom and of the offspring to come,
Abram longs to hasten being a father, but his chaste wife
declines the duty, which her worn-out old age shows to be vain,
the sign having already ceased; but believing that a sweet pledge
for her husband and a new hope, born of whatever concubine,
would be her own, she puts in her place her maidservant, younger in years —
Hagar was her name, the land of the Nile her origin —
into the marriage bed, and, approaching her husband with entreaties,
persuaded him to entrust his progeny to a lowly womb.
Oh, the wickedness of a slave! As soon as Hagar felt the burden of her womb
come alive, swollen with arrogant pride
she despised her mistress, the mistress to whom she owed
a mother's love, and, in her frenzy, the very cause of her swelling.
Rightly therefore Abram, most just of men, handed her over to the lashes
of his wife; and driven more by the shame of them,
she hides herself, indignant, in deserts far away and the secret lairs
of wild beasts; nor did she flee for what she had suffered,
but, feigning excessive fears, she once again
scorns her mistress in the only way she can, and prefers to bear the dangers
of a lonely road — had not an angel, sent from heaven,
met her and restored the servant to her former place
under a gentle mistress, and, having revived her with great
encouragement, bidden her on her return to hope for better things,
and told her the name of her son, his ways and deeds,
and the countless throngs of people from the stock of his descendants.
She returns with greater longing, now sure of the future,
and by giving birth she was the first to make her lord a father,
when, the happy span of his life already run,
he was completing eighty years and six besides.
When he had added thirteen summers to the course thus begun,
the gracious Father again came to him, deigning
his customary address, and bade him, trembling,
to live in blessedness; at the same time he went over again the promises
which were the reward of his virtue — then, with body bowed,
Abram, prostrate in supplication, worships the Lord —
and after many words, by which he eased the longings
of his faithful servant, he commanded him to set himself apart from all peoples
by a silent sign, so that, the superfluous flesh willingly cut away,
it might be plain, readily and clearly,
that the Lord had commanded, with bodily vices cut off,
that a new progeny and offspring to come be preserved.
The thing itself speaks without words: that God thus commanded
the private parts to be cut, and that boys fresh from their mother
and new to life, while the mind does not yet know pain,
should be stripped of the foreskin and consecrated on the eighth day;
and that whoever dared to violate so holy a covenant,
failing to submit to the law laid upon him,
would be disinherited from the kingdom and the life to come.
And at the same time, so that he might believe on true proof
that countless nations would be created from his own stock,
so that their names might proclaim this very thing, he changed them and said:
"Let a letter renew you, let a fuller syllable remake you,
so that your wife be called not Sara but Sarra,
and you not Abram, but, made more illustrious by an enlarged name,
be called Abraham from now on by peoples to come.
This promise you share with your wife in truth,
since, as the ages roll on through time,
she will be the mother of the race, and when the sun has measured out the year again
she will make you a father. Though you may think laughable
the promises of my power, since your old age
raises its objection, it will be the glory of divine right
that it be thought possible exactly as I shall have performed it.
Yet I will pardon the doubters, and on the son to come
I will lay a name that will rebuke this fault, Isaac,
who alone, with all the stock of his descendants, will be
my sure heir, the terms of the covenant kept.
Yet Ishmael here, whom alone you now embrace,
shall not be without a share of the holy dowry; for, upheld by my gift,
he will bring forth many thousands of men, nations of strong lineage,
to be ruled by twelve chieftains together."
He spoke; and Abraham, eager to hasten the covenant he had received,
now nearing a hundred years, his son now come of age,
first himself and his son, and then all his dependents
and servants he sets apart from the age by the sign, as commanded,
and makes them a new people and a fountain of the godly,
in one and the same act — so great is his devotion — receiving
and fulfilling the law of God. What would such ready
and swift faith not deserve? This is no longer fear,
but sincere love and the full proof of a servant:
to submit to any command with so calm a mind
that God is glad to have commanded it. For before, accustomed only
to be heard, after such merit in his minister
he now allows himself to be seen, and even when just indignation
spurs him to vengeance, in his gentle divinity he does not
refuse the sight of mortals. For when he was preparing to condemn
the crimes of the earth and to destroy the guilty with flames,
either as he truly was or in such form as he knew he could be seen,
declaring his divinity and his number to his foster son,
though he came accompanied by heavenly servants,
he presented himself to view. For as Abraham sat beside his dwelling,
three suddenly stood before him, shining with majestic light.
Abraham, stirred by the appearance of so great a sight,
runs forward and, prostrate on the ground, worships the Lord
as one, though he marvels at three, and, eager to please,
he begs that he may be allowed to serve with devout mind,
that, as the hours were stretching on into midday heat, they would not disdain
to be refreshed by their servant with table and food.
So far did he waver in doubt between what he saw and his lively senses,
because the form showed a man
whom his mind knew to be God. Yet the Almighty nodded assent
and does not spurn the service of his devoted foster son,
and is seen to hallow the food and the table,
so that his devoted minister might believe his gifts accepted;
a pure and radiant image of the priest appears,
an image that would show that a true man, in face and whole body,
would one day be taken on by God, and give proofs of Christ to come,
and that, unfolding wondrous promises,
it might declare them and, being present, forbid his servant to doubt.
Then, setting out, the host keeps close at the side of his departing guests,
rejoicing, and a sweet dread shakes his stricken
breast, and a reverent awe draws him on, astonished.
For he sees that God had turned silent looks and stern glances
toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and at the same time
had sent forth his servants, ministers of peace and of wrath;
and when he had learned what God was preparing with such great effort,
as God revealed his secrets and taught him the reason
for his coming — so that he who had learned what rewards of life
await the elect might also beware of what is to be feared —
he dared of his own accord to ask the Lord whether he would destroy the city
of an erring people for all the crimes of the guilty
if perhaps it held fifty upright citizens.
"I will not destroy it," he said. Then gentle questioning,
bringing the number down little by little and pressing for pardon
humbly, lowering the totals with each return,
won the Father's answer all the way down to ten;
and, lest the mild Lord's clemency
reveal itself entirely, he left his servant in mid-speech,
still pressing further, and withdrew into his own realm.
Meanwhile those sent to Sodom find Lot by chance sitting
before the gates of the city, as the sun was already nearing the earth.
When he saw with wondrous splendor
the angelic men shining, thinking they had come from heaven
— for God himself gave him understanding — he worships them prostrate
and invites them home, and by his entreaties prevails on them to spend the night
under his roof, and at the same time persuades them to dine with him,
and serves them wholesome food and sparing cups.
Behold, toward the setting of the light and the return of night,
a foul band of the populace — of males, if it is right to say so —
bursts forth, and boys and old men vie in sharpening
the frenzies of the young: they call on Lot by name with loud cries
to hand over those he had received. It is shameful, alas, and surely it is better
to keep silent about so great a wickedness than to publish it in words,
even while condemning it — a thing which even then, by perverse custom,
was the law of that unspeakable city. Wishing to calm the raging men,
Lot offers his daughters, in whom their native
virginity still remained, for whatever uses the mob might wish,
meaning, through their sex, to commit a lesser wrong. But profane hearts
think cheap whatever is permitted and delight in being forbidden,
so that there may be something to desire. So they strive to assault
the man himself, champion of faith, teacher of morals and of justice.
When the violence was now greater than human effort
could drive back by strength, then both guests
lay bare their angelic powers, their feigned bodies set aside,
and draw Lot back, snatching him away, and strike the raging men blind.
The sentence of justice kept the custom of law:
coming before the punishment, it closed the eyes of the condemned.
Then to Lot, trembling and scarcely in his right mind again,
the holy ministers, not concealing their nature,
since he had already sensed in his heart what he himself also feared,
declare who they are, why they have come, what their orders are,
and what they intend to do. If his sons-in-law are worthy to believe,
let Lot tell them of the destruction; for he was commanded to escape
and to gather his mixed household, whose name [?] among many,
and his sons-in-law; but their base origin did not deserve
to feel the fear of God. Yet let no one think them alone
slow of faith, since Lot too hesitates
to leave his home. When, as daylight drew near,
both guests see him hesitating and dragging out sluggish delays without end,
they seize him by the hands along with his wife
and his virgin daughters and lead him far outside the walls,
and bid him hurry and escape into the high mountains,
laying down this law: that none should look back at what he had passed,
wrongly cautious. But Lot, fearing
that the swift wrath of punishment might overtake him in his slowness,
himself begged with tears for Segor, and his asking pleased,
because it moved the Lord to save many at once,
and he shared the special gift of salvation granted to himself
with others, and made merit out of a gift.
And now clouds, swiftly covering the sky, compelled
by the Father's power as God stirred them together,
had thickened into mists not of the usual kind, but such as Etna whirls aloft,
such as Inarime vomits, such as Aponus breathes out with its hot waters,
such as the earth, shaken by neighboring Vesuvius,
belches forth, such as the savage mouths of the Lycian Chimaera
pant out from the vast hollow of their triple furnace,
and wherever a swift wind, kindling hidden sulphur
and forced through a narrow channel,
streams out into the light, steaming from the broken earth.
Not that he could not have turned the rains, too, into fire,
he who was free to found the whole world from nothing;
but the good judge prefers to condemn with greater preparation
those whom, in pity for the ruin of the world and of morals,
he punishes as an example. So everything from every shore
rushes together in a billowing mass, and, packed tight by its own blast,
every kind of fuel for flame comes together into one,
and, like a solid body, a curved vault of sulphurous matter
covers the lands and the guilty cities;
and the wind, swift and gathering strength in its narrow channel,
struck it and forced it to crackle with so great a crash,
and, with thunder echoing the frequent lightning,
to dismay their minds, so that Lot's wretched wife,
trembling, turned and cast her eyes back, as was forbidden,
and suffered swift punishment for breaking the law,
turned into a statue of salt; and, robbed of light,
the unhappy woman lost her life together with her whole body,
so that, though her shape remained, no corpse was left.
Then more swiftly, with fear driving out grief,
Lot enters Segor, stunned by the horrifying calamity.
And the sun rises, hotter with all its fire,
flashing with angry brightness, and aims its stern rays
at Sodom. After they had wrapped the daylight
in their flames, and the melted sulphur hurled down
the fires bound up within it, and with dry liquid
the blazes drip down, spread out in their own beds [?],
a lightning-laden storm falls headlong from the thick air
and engulfs the cities and rages over all the fields,
and thunders with mingled roar, and the fiery tempest
drowns their cries; and after it had found fuel
in the overwhelmed lands and settled on the very sands,
the fire, its fuel joined together, raises a vast cone,
and flames return from the earth to the stars,
until the rocks and the bursting earth
pass into ashes, and the sunken sands are utterly dissolved,
and, the turf consumed and the fields sunk down,
the land opens hollow basins, and the moisture that had bound the earth,
pouring out from its opened veins and joining its forces,
gives birth to a sea of its own. What are we to think it means
that a lake is suddenly filled by wondrous power
where before there was a pyre? Did the good judge wish to destroy
the condemned with every element, or does gentle clemency rather
silently mark an end to the punishment
in quenching the flames with waters? And perhaps a substance
opposed to heat foreshows the respite of the judgment to come,
as does the holy Jordan flowing into the lake,
which first was found worthy to wash away the sins of men.
